scenario_constructions: Kwame Osei and the seven-university consortium are fictional, invented for this case -- consistent with the corpus convention used for e.g. Rosa Delgado / the Fermenter case and Dana Okafor / Turbine Channel.

The lease-option window's remaining length (Background) is set to five days -- a scenario detail with no real citable source, consistent with the Overview's 'close Friday' urgency, disclosed as a stated scenario detail rather than sourced externally.

Vantage Mesa and Sable Hollow are fictional sites explicitly modeled on two real, named astronomical sites' real published astroclimate statistics (ESO's Paranal and the Isaac Newton Group's La Palma site, S1/S3) -- the fictional names/geography are invented, but the clear-sky fractions driving every downstream calculation are real, cited data, not invented.

modeling_assumptions.basis: No public spec exists for this hypothetical composite dome accessory; fixed in proportion to the drum's real 2.5 m radius so the windscreen reads as a plausible small structure, not a decorative add-on.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Low. The windscreen is the smallest of the three shell components by volume at both sites; even a large change to its height moves total construction cost only slightly, since the drum and dome dominate the steel total.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Wind-driven shell-thickness reinforcement factor (Vantage Mesa's design wind speed 100 mph, divided by Sable Hollow's 70 mph = 1.4286x), applied to the drum wall, dome cap, and windscreen shell thicknesses
modeling_assumptions.basis: The two design wind speeds are real, cited HUD figures (S5), used as a stated stand-in for 'standard' vs. 'reinforced' wind design since no public wind-zone rating exists for small observatory domes. The scaling relationship itself -- wind pressure scales with the square of wind speed, and the shell thickness needed to hold bending stress constant under a given pressure scales with the square root of that pressure, so thickness scales directly with the speed ratio -- is a standard, general structural-engineering simplification, not a case-specific citation.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: This is the single most dilemma-relevant assumption in the case. sensitivity_model.py's mechanical +/-50% sweep (2026-09-18) confirms this is genuinely load-bearing: at -50% (factor 0.7143) the winner FLIPS from B (Sable Hollow) to A (Vantage Mesa), margin 26.79%, breaching SPEC Section 2's 20% cap; at +50% (factor 2.1429) the winner stays B but the margin widens to 38.12%, also breaching the cap. Both directions breach the cap; one direction also flips the recommendation outright.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Pyramidal pier footing dimensions (3.0 m base side, 1.0 m height), identical at both sites
modeling_assumptions.value_used: 3.0 m x 3.0 m base, 1.0 m height, both sites
modeling_assumptions.basis: No public spec exists for a footing at this exact hypothetical scale. Grounded in the real, documented design principle that telescope piers are conventionally oversized for mass/stiffness (vibration damping at the optical axis) rather than sized to bearing capacity alone -- a real consideration in both professional and amateur observatory construction literature.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: None on the balance test -- identical at both sites by construction, so it adds equally to both options' total cost and cannot change which option wins. Disclosed because it is an unsourced, stated dimension, not because it is dilemma-relevant.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Average usable hours of darkness per clear night, both sites
modeling_assumptions.basis: No single, directly-fetchable primary source stated an annual-average dark-time figure for either real modeled site (a specific seasonal-range claim was investigated and dropped -- see not_found[] and excluded_sources[]). 9.0 hours is a round, disclosed planning figure for a subtropical-latitude astronomical site's typical usable dark time per night, applied identically at both sites since both real modeled sites sit at broadly comparable subtropical latitudes (24-28 degrees).
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: None on the balance test -- applied identically at both sites, so it scales both options' usable-hours figure by the same factor and cannot, by construction, change which option wins (confirmed: margin_pct is unchanged whether this value is 9.0 or the earlier candidate 9.05).

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Cross-site clear-sky category comparability -- treating Appendix A's 77% 'Photometric + Clear' (ground-based) figure as comparable to Appendix B's 62.6% 'clear' (ground-based) figure
modeling_assumptions.basis: No single real monitoring program publishes both real sites' statistics under one shared category definition. Both figures are each site's own ground-based-instrument 'clear enough to observe' measurement -- the closest real matching pair of the several categories each site publishes (Appendix B alone reports four different real figures, from just over 50% to 71.9%, depending on definition and measurement method). Appendix A and Appendix B both flag this openly.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Added 2026-09-18 following a Tier 2 P4 adversarial finding, then RE-VERIFIED and its own underlying S3 figure CORRECTED 2026-09-18 during Tier 2 P6 data-decay verification (a direct fetch found the paper does not state the figures an earlier draft cited -- see sources[S3]). In the BASE case this assumption is secondary (Argument B does not depend on it -- the construction-cost gap alone decides the base case, though now by a much thinner margin, 4.79%). Under the case's Twist, this assumption becomes fully determinative -- once the twist equalizes construction cost at both sites, the entire recommendation rests on treating 77% and 62.6% (a ~14-point gap) as comparable, or on which of Appendix B's four published figures a Hero argues is the fairer match.

sensitivity_note: SPEC Section 6 does not apply -- this is a siting/capital-expenditure decision with no death, illness, or family-hardship stakes.

balance.argument_a: Vantage Mesa has a real, published clear-sky advantage: 77% Photometric+Clear nights (long-term ESO Paranal-modeled figure) versus Sable Hollow's 70% clear-night fraction -- a real ~10% more usable nights per year, and the traditional siting instinct is that more clear sky always wins for a survey telescope, since raw observing time is the whole point of the program.
balance.argument_b: Sable Hollow wins on this case's actual computed primary metric, though narrowly. Vantage Mesa's higher HUD-analog design wind speed (100 mph vs. 70 mph) requires shell steel roughly 1.43x thicker throughout the drum, dome cap, and windscreen (Appendix D, MA2) -- pushing total dome-and-pier construction cost from $3,994.15 at Sable Hollow to $5,159.99 at Vantage Mesa, a 29% cost increase for only a ~23% gain in usable hours (Vantage Mesa's real clear-sky advantage widened once S3's figure was corrected to its verified 62.6%, not the earlier unverified 70%). Sable Hollow delivers 0.5148 usable clear-sky hours per dollar versus Vantage Mesa's 0.4902 -- Sable Hollow wins by 4.79%, well inside SPEC Section 2's ~20% cap and close to the corpus's own 'gold standard' thin-margin precedent (Robotics Engineering, 0.09%).
balance.margin_basis: Computed by case-research from real cited astroclimate fractions (Appendix A/B), real Ash-Dome-derived shell dimensions and thicknesses (Appendix C/D), and real 2026 material unit prices (Appendix F). Usable hours/year = clear-sky fraction x average usable dark hours per clear night (9.0 h, a disclosed planning assumption MA4, applied identically at both sites) x 365. Construction cost = steel cost (shell volumes via outer-minus-inner solid subtraction, converted to mass via steel density, converted to cost via steel price) + concrete cost (pier volume x concrete price) + formwork cost (pier LATERAL surface area only x formwork price -- the footing's base sits against undisturbed soil and needs no form, per Appendix E's construction note). margin_pct = |metric_A - metric_B| / max(metric_A, metric_B) x 100. Full arithmetic in RESEARCH_LOG.md.
balance.twist_effect: The insurer's uniform minimum wind rating forces Sable Hollow to also pay the reinforced $5,159.99 construction cost, erasing its cost advantage entirely. With both options paying the same denominator, the comparison collapses to whichever option has more usable hours per year -- Vantage Mesa's 2,529.45 h beats Sable Hollow's 2,056.41 h outright, flipping the winner from B to A at an 18.70% margin (still inside the 20% cap). Verified mechanically via sensitivity_model.py's evaluate_twist(). Per P4 adversarial review (2026-09-18), this flip's validity rests entirely on MA5 (cross-site clear-sky category comparability) -- see case.json.modeling_assumptions[MA5] and FACILITATOR.md's Twist section.

deliverables.text: A surface-area table for the cylindrical drum wall: total exterior surface area used for the wall's protective coating, in square meters, computed from the drum's radius and height, with formula and work shown.

A shell-volume table for the drum wall and the windscreen: for each option, the volume of steel in the cylindrical drum wall and in the conical windscreen, each computed as the outer-radius solid's volume minus the inner-radius solid's volume, converted to mass and to steel cost.

A shell-volume table for the dome cap: for each option, the volume of steel in the hemispherical dome cap, computed explicitly as half the volume of a full sphere of the same radius (outer minus inner), converted to mass and to steel cost.

A pier-footing table: the total surface area of the pyramidal pier footing (base plus all four triangular lateral faces), the lateral (four-face-only) surface area used specifically for formwork cost, and the total volume (for concrete cost), with formulas and work shown for all three.

A clear-sky probability table: for each option, the expected number of clear-sky nights per year and the probability of a specific run of consecutive clear nights (e.g. a clear five-night observing week), modeled explicitly as independent yes/no trials.

A final usable-hours-per-dollar table: for each option, total dome-and-pier construction cost (from D1-D4), total usable clear-sky observing hours per year (from D5's expected-nights figure and each site's average usable hours of darkness per clear night), and the resulting usable hours per dollar, with every unit conversion shown.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: reinforcement_factor (MA2, 1.4286x = 100mph/70mph) is a good-faith scenario stand-in built from two real, cited HUD wind-zone design speeds (S5) combined with a standard, general structural-engineering thickness-vs-pressure scaling relationship -- not a manufacturer-published wind rating for this class of dome, since no public spec exists (see not_found[]). sensitivity_model.py's mechanical +/-50% sweep (2026-09-18 run, re-run after S3's correction) confirms this is genuinely load-bearing, not a scoping artifact: at -50% (factor 0.7143) the winner FLIPS from B (Sable Hollow) to A (Vantage Mesa) and the margin widens to 34.53%, breaching SPEC Section 2's 20% balance cap; at +50% (factor 2.1429) the winner stays B but the margin widens to 30.81%, also breaching the 20% cap. Both directions breach the cap; one direction also flips the recommendation outright. This is disclosed here in full, not softened -- MA2 is the single most fragile, dilemma-relevant assumption in the case, and a Hero who challenges this specific factor is raising exactly the right question. See case.json.modeling_assumptions[MA2] and FACILITATOR.md for the same finding in prose.

facilitator.twist: The consortium's insurer requires every site to carry the same minimum wind rating regardless of local exposure -- Sable Hollow must now also be built to the reinforced (100 mph) spec, erasing its cost advantage and flipping the recommendation to Vantage Mesa.

P7_waiver.reason: Four remediation rounds each produced a verified, real improvement: round 1 added inline plain-language glosses for 10 named real-world terms and a hand-verified SVG cross-section diagram of the composite enclosure (previously nonexistent); round 2 fixed a genuine geometric-plausibility problem in the windscreen's description and diagram (a cone's flat base cannot sit flush against a curved wall -- added a real, standard flat mounting bracket); round 3 fixed a genuine structural-plausibility problem in the footing's description and diagram (apex meeting the drum at a single point is not how real footings bear load -- redrawn wide-base-down with a riser, and disclosed the full-pyramid shape itself as a stated simplification of a real truncated-footing form); round 4 fixed the shutter slit's mechanism description (a vague 'slides open' become an explicit retracting panel on a track). Each round's cold-read confirmed the specific prior finding was resolved, even as a new, narrower one emerged. This pattern -- genuine convergence on each specific finding, without reaching zero total findings -- matches the doctrine's own documented experience with other domain-rich composite-scenario cases (carpenter, codebreaker), where SKILL.md itself records that 'fixing where the packet comes from does not manufacture a PASS that isn't earned.' Waiving per MCS-49 rather than treating continued, narrowing findings as a case-write defect that blocks TIER2_PASS indefinitely.
